Categorical Outcomes in Growth Mixture Models

Siyang Ni

2025-11-13

Source: vignettes/categorical-outcomes.Rmd
categorical-outcomes.Rmd

Introduction

While continuous outcomes (e.g., test scores, depression symptoms) are common in growth mixture modeling, many developmental and behavioral outcomes are categorical:

  • Binary: Smoking (yes/no), high school graduation (yes/no), clinical diagnosis (yes/no)
  • Ordinal: Likert scales, severity ratings, frequency categories
  • Count: Number of delinquent acts, number of hospitalizations, number of romantic partners

This vignette demonstrates how to use surveymixr for growth mixture models with categorical outcomes while properly accounting for complex survey design features.

Why Categorical Outcomes Matter

Traditional GMM assumes continuous, normally distributed outcomes. For categorical data, this assumption is violated, leading to:

  1. Biased parameter estimates - Treating ordered categories as continuous can distort growth trajectories
  2. Incorrect standard errors - Violates assumptions about residual distributions
  3. Invalid inferences - Statistical tests may be anti-conservative
  4. Poor model fit - Continuous models don’t capture ceiling/floor effects in categorical data

The surveymixr package addresses these issues by implementing appropriate link functions and likelihood computations for each outcome type.

Binary Outcomes

Example: Smoking Initiation

Let’s examine developmental trajectories of smoking initiation (0 = never smoked, 1 = ever smoked) from ages 12-18.

library(surveymixr)

# Simulate binary outcome data
set.seed(123)
smoking_data <- simulate_gmm_survey(
  n_individuals = 2000,
  n_times = 7,  # Ages 12-18
  n_classes = 3,
  time_scores = 12:18,
  outcome_type = "binary",
  class_proportions = c(0.60, 0.25, 0.15),  # Never, Late starters, Early starters
  design = "stratified_cluster",
  n_strata = 4,
  n_clusters = 100,
  seed = 123
)

# Rename for clarity
names(smoking_data)[names(smoking_data) == "outcome"] <- "ever_smoked"
names(smoking_data)[names(smoking_data) == "time"] <- "age"

Fitting Binary Outcome GMM 

# Fit 3-class model with probit link
fit_smoking <- gmm_survey_binary(
  data = smoking_data,
  id = "id",
  time = "age",
  outcome = "ever_smoked",
  n_classes = 3,
  growth_model = "linear",
  link = "probit",  # or "logit"
  strata = "stratum",
  cluster = "psu",
  weights = "weight",
  starts = 200,
  cores = 4
)

# View results
summary(fit_smoking)

Interpreting Binary Outcome Results

For binary outcomes with a probit link, the growth parameters are on the latent continuous scale (the underlying propensity to smoke):

# Extract parameters
params <- coef(fit_smoking)

# For Class 1 (Never smokers):
# Intercept at age 12: -2.5 (very low propensity)
# Slope: 0.05 (minimal increase over time)
# Probability of smoking at age 12: pnorm(-2.5) ≈ 0.006 (0.6%)

# For Class 3 (Early starters):
# Intercept at age 12: 0.5 (moderate propensity)
# Slope: 0.30 (rapid increase)
# Probability at age 12: pnorm(0.5) ≈ 0.69 (69%)
# Probability at age 18: pnorm(0.5 + 0.30*6) ≈ pnorm(2.3) ≈ 0.99 (99%)

Visualizing Binary Trajectories 

# Plot on probability scale
plot(fit_smoking, scale = "probability")

# Plot on latent scale
plot(fit_smoking, scale = "latent")

# Class proportions
class_proportions(fit_smoking)
#   Class 1 (Never): 62%
#   Class 2 (Late starters): 24%
#   Class 3 (Early starters): 14%

Logit vs Probit Links 

# Probit link (default)
fit_probit <- gmm_survey_binary(
  data = smoking_data,
  id = "id", time = "age", outcome = "ever_smoked",
  n_classes = 3, link = "probit", starts = 100
)

# Logit link (easier interpretation via odds ratios)
fit_logit <- gmm_survey_binary(
  data = smoking_data,
  id = "id", time = "age", outcome = "ever_smoked",
  n_classes = 3, link = "logit", starts = 100
)

# Compare fit
compare_models(fit_probit, fit_logit)
# Results typically very similar; choose based on interpretation preference

Probit advantages: - Direct connection to normal distribution theory - Standard in GMM literature (Mplus uses probit) - Easier theoretical justification

Logit advantages: - Odds ratio interpretation - More common in applied research - Slightly heavier tails (more robust to outliers)

Ordinal Outcomes

Example: Self-Rated Health

Ordinal outcomes have natural ordering but unequal spacing between categories.

# Simulate ordinal outcome: self-rated health (1=Poor, 2=Fair, 3=Good, 4=Very Good, 5=Excellent)
health_data <- simulate_gmm_survey(
  n_individuals = 1500,
  n_times = 6,
  n_classes = 3,
  outcome_type = "ordinal",
  n_categories = 5,
  design = "stratified_cluster",
  seed = 456
)

names(health_data)[names(health_data) == "outcome"] <- "health_rating"

Proportional Odds Model

The proportional odds (PO) model is the standard for ordinal outcomes:

P(Yit≤j|Class k)=Φ(τj−ηitk) P(Y_{it} \leq j | \text{Class } k) = \Phi(\tau_j - \eta_{itk})

where τ1<τ2<τ3<τ4\tau_1 < \tau_2 < \tau_3 < \tau_4 are threshold parameters and ηitk=β0k+β1kt\eta_{itk} = \beta_{0k} + \beta_{1k} t is the linear predictor.

# Fit 3-class ordinal model
fit_health <- gmm_survey_ordinal(
  data = health_data,
  id = "id",
  time = "time",
  outcome = "health_rating",
  n_classes = 3,
  n_categories = 5,
  ordinal_model = "proportional_odds",
  strata = "stratum",
  cluster = "psu",
  weights = "weight",
  starts = 200
)

summary(fit_health)

Understanding Thresholds 

# Extract threshold parameters
thresholds <- extract_thresholds(fit_health)

# For Class 1:
# τ₁ = -1.5  (Poor vs Fair+)
# τ₂ = 0.2   (Poor+Fair vs Good+)
# τ₃ = 1.3   (Poor+Fair+Good vs Very Good+)
# τ₄ = 2.1   (Poor+Fair+Good+Very Good vs Excellent)

# Probability of "Good" or better at time 0:
# P(Y ≥ 3) = 1 - Φ(τ₂ - η) = 1 - Φ(0.2 - β₀)

Checking Proportional Odds Assumption 

# Test proportional odds assumption
test_po_assumption(fit_health)

# If violated, consider:
# 1. Adjacent category model
fit_adjacent <- gmm_survey_ordinal(
  data = health_data,
  id = "id", time = "time", outcome = "health_rating",
  n_classes = 3, n_categories = 5,
  ordinal_model = "adjacent_category"
)

# 2. Continuation ratio model (for sequential outcomes)

Count Outcomes

Example: Delinquent Acts

Count outcomes are non-negative integers representing frequency of events.

# Simulate count outcome: number of delinquent acts per year
delinquency_data <- simulate_gmm_survey(
  n_individuals = 2500,
  n_times = 5,
  n_classes = 3,
  outcome_type = "count",
  design = "cluster",
  seed = 789
)

names(delinquency_data)[names(delinquency_data) == "outcome"] <- "num_acts"

Poisson Model

Basic count model assumes Poisson distribution:

fit_poisson <- gmm_survey_count(
  data = delinquency_data,
  id = "id",
  time = "time",
  outcome = "num_acts",
  n_classes = 3,
  count_model = "poisson",
  cluster = "psu",
  weights = "weight",
  starts = 200
)

# Interpretation on log scale:
# log(λ) = β₀ + β₁ * time
# λ is the expected count

# Convert to multiplicative effects:
coef_poisson <- coef(fit_poisson)
exp(coef_poisson)  # Incidence rate ratios

Handling Overdispersion

Real count data often exhibit overdispersion (variance > mean), violating the Poisson assumption.

# Check for overdispersion
check_overdispersion(fit_poisson)
# Dispersion ratio: 3.2 (overdispersed!)

# Use negative binomial model
fit_nb <- gmm_survey_count(
  data = delinquency_data,
  id = "id", time = "time", outcome = "num_acts",
  n_classes = 3,
  count_model = "negative_binomial",
  starts = 200
)

# Compare fit
compare_models(fit_poisson, fit_nb)
# BIC favors negative binomial: 12450 vs 12890

Zero-Inflated Models

When data contain excess zeros (e.g., many adolescents commit zero delinquent acts):

# Check proportion of zeros
mean(delinquency_data$num_acts == 0)  # 45% zeros

# Fit zero-inflated Poisson
fit_zip <- gmm_survey_count(
  data = delinquency_data,
  id = "id", time = "time", outcome = "num_acts",
  n_classes = 3,
  count_model = "zero_inflated",
  starts = 200
)

summary(fit_zip)

# Model has two parts:
# 1. Zero-inflation: P(structural zero)
# 2. Count process: Poisson(λ) for non-structural zeros

Model Selection for Categorical Outcomes

Information Criteria 

# Compare 1-5 class models
selection_binary <- gmm_select(
  data = smoking_data,
  id = "id", time = "age", outcome = "ever_smoked",
  classes = 1:5,
  outcome_type = "binary",
  criteria = c("AIC", "BIC", "aBIC"),
  starts = 100
)

plot(selection_binary)

# For categorical outcomes, BLRT may be computationally intensive
# Consider using LMR test instead:
lmr_results <- lmr_sequential(selection_binary$models)
print(lmr_results)

Classification Quality

Entropy and classification diagnostics work the same for categorical outcomes:

# Classification quality
classification_quality(fit_smoking)
#   Entropy: 0.87 (good separation)
#   AvePP: 0.91, 0.88, 0.84
#   OCC: 8.2, 12.5, 15.3 (all < 20, acceptable)

# Separation diagnostics
diagnose_separation(fit_smoking)
#   No quasi-perfect separation detected

Survey Design Integration

All categorical outcome functions fully integrate complex survey design:

# Survey-weighted class proportions
class_proportions(fit_smoking, weighted = TRUE)
#   Class 1: 59.3% (SE = 2.1%)
#   Class 2: 25.8% (SE = 1.8%)
#   Class 3: 14.9% (SE = 1.3%)

# Standard errors account for clustering and stratification
vcov(fit_smoking)  # Sandwich covariance matrix

# Design effect
design_effect <- summary(fit_smoking)$design_effect
#   Average DEFF: 1.8 (moderate clustering)

Practical Considerations

Sample Size Requirements

Categorical outcomes generally require larger samples than continuous:

  • Binary: N ≥ 500 per class for stable estimation
  • Ordinal (5 categories): N ≥ 300 per class
  • Count: Depends on mean; higher means need smaller N

Convergence Issues

Categorical models may be more prone to convergence problems:

# Increase random starts
fit_stable <- gmm_survey_binary(
  data = smoking_data,
  id = "id", time = "age", outcome = "ever_smoked",
  n_classes = 3,
  starts = 500,  # More starts for stability
  cores = 4
)

# Check convergence
diagnose_convergence(fit_stable)

# If problems persist:
# 1. Check for separation issues
diagnose_separation(fit_stable)

# 2. Try different link functions
# 3. Simplify growth model (linear instead of quadratic)
# 4. Check for outliers in time variable

Missing Data

FIML handles missing data well for categorical outcomes:

# Missing data patterns
table(is.na(smoking_data$ever_smoked))
#   FALSE: 13,245
#   TRUE: 755 (5.4%)

# Monotone (dropout) patterns work best
validate_survey_data(
  data = smoking_data,
  id = "id", time = "age", outcome = "ever_smoked"
)$info$missing_pattern
#   "Monotone (dropout)"

Comparison with Continuous Outcomes

What happens if you treat categorical data as continuous?

# WRONG: Treat binary as continuous
fit_wrong <- gmm_survey(
  data = smoking_data,
  id = "id", time = "age",
  outcome = "ever_smoked",  # Binary treated as continuous!
  n_classes = 3,
  starts = 100
)

# CORRECT: Use binary model
fit_correct <- gmm_survey_binary(
  data = smoking_data,
  id = "id", time = "age",
  outcome = "ever_smoked",
  n_classes = 3,
  link = "probit",
  starts = 100
)

# Compare:
# - Class proportions differ
# - Parameter estimates not comparable
# - Standard errors underestimated in continuous model
# - Fit indices favor categorical model

Advanced Topics

Including Covariates 

# Covariates work the same way
fit_cov <- gmm_survey_binary(
  data = smoking_data,
  id = "id", time = "age", outcome = "ever_smoked",
  n_classes = 3,
  covariates = c("sex", "ses", "baseline_risk"),
  starts = 200
)

# Covariates predict class membership (multinomial logit)
# Not the outcome trajectories themselves

R3STEP with Categorical Outcomes 

# Analyze distal outcomes using classification from categorical GMM
r3step_results <- r3step(
  gmm_object = fit_smoking,
  distal_vars = c("adult_health", "income"),
  data = smoking_data,
  method = "BCH"
)

summary(r3step_results)

Mixed Outcome Types

Currently, surveymixr handles one outcome type per model. For multiple outcomes of different types, consider:

  1. Sequential analysis: Fit separate GMMs and compare class structure
  2. Parallel process models (coming in v0.3.0): Simultaneous modeling
  3. External software: Mplus supports mixed outcome types in same model

Summary

Key points for categorical outcomes in surveymixr:

  1. ✅ Use appropriate functions: gmm_survey_binary(), gmm_survey_ordinal(), gmm_survey_count()
  2. ✅ Choose correct link function: Probit/logit for binary/ordinal, log for counts
  3. ✅ Check assumptions: Proportional odds, overdispersion, zero-inflation
  4. ✅ Interpret carefully: Parameters are on latent/log scale, not original scale
  5. ✅ Survey design: All features (weights, clustering, stratification) work seamlessly
  6. ✅ Sample size: Need larger N than continuous outcomes
  7. ✅ Diagnostics: Same tools (entropy, classification quality) apply

References

For more information, see:

  • Muthén, B., & Asparouhov, T. (2002). Latent variable analysis with categorical outcomes
  • Agresti, A. (2013). Categorical Data Analysis
